opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we think about a lot. The first thing I'd say is that real conflicts are rarer than people expect. Most of the time, when a commercial user wants something, a faster kernel for a certain model, better support for some hardware, more stable APIs, the broader community wants it too. A company deploying at scale is often just hitting the problems everyone will hit a few months later.

When there is genuine tension, our guiding principle is that the open-source project has to stay general. We don't want the core codebase shaped around one customer's private setup. So when a company asks for something very specific to their internal infrastructure, we usually say: let's figure out the general abstraction underneath this. Maybe it's a plugin interface, maybe a cleaner extension point, so you can implement your special logic on your side without forcing everyone else to carry that complexity. That has pushed us to make the architecture more modular, which helps the whole ecosystem.

Second, we're quite firm that money doesn't buy a merge. Companies can sponsor development, contribute engineers, and send PRs, and we really appreciate that. But the code goes through the same review process as anyone else's. If a change makes the system harder to maintain or hurts other users, it doesn't go in as is, regardless of who wrote it. I think contributors respect that, because the reason they chose an open-source engine is that it's neutral. If it became one company's tool, it would lose the value they came for.

Third, there's a time-horizon question. Sometimes a customer needs something tomorrow, and the community's proper solution will take a month. In that case it's totally fine for them to carry a patch or a fork for a while, and we try to upstream the right version later. We just try to make sure forks don't drift so far that they can't come back.

So the short answer: keep the core general, provide extension points for the specific stuff, treat everyone's code by the same standard, and be honest when the community's priorities differ from a particular company's. In the long run, a healthy open-source project serves commercial users better than one bent to fit any single one of them.

r001.rationale: The response describes keeping the project general and applying the same review standards, but does not say they decline commercial customers with conflicting needs.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that limited capacity to serve customers enables them to turn down unwanted work.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, in vLLM we don't really treat them as two separate groups, because the line between them is blurry. Many of our most active contributors are themselves employees of commercial companies. Someone from a cloud provider or a chip vendor submits a PR because their customers need it, and at the same time that PR becomes part of the open-source project that everyone uses. So the "commercial customer" and the "community member" are often the same person.

That said, there are real tensions. A company might come to us and say, we need this feature next week, our product launch depends on it. From the project's perspective, we have to ask: does this feature benefit general users, or does it only serve one company's specific setup? If it adds a lot of complexity to the codebase for a narrow use case, we tend to push back, or we ask them to keep it as a plugin or an external extension rather than merging it into the core. We've been deliberately building more plugin interfaces over the past year precisely because of this. It lets companies move fast on their own needs without forcing their choices on everyone else.

The second tension is about priorities and timing. Open-source maintainers have limited bandwidth, and we can't let the loudest or richest party decide the roadmap. What we try to do is be transparent. We have a public roadmap, public RFCs, and the discussions happen in the open. If a company wants something prioritized, the healthiest way is for them to contribute engineers to do the work and to review others' work too, not just to file requests. Companies that invest in the project in this way naturally gain influence, and I think that's fair, because they're also carrying the maintenance burden.

The third thing, and I think this is the most important, is being honest about what we won't do. We won't keep a private fork with better features for paying customers. The moment the open version becomes a second-class product, the community's trust is gone, and that trust is really the only asset an open-source project has. So when a commercial need genuinely conflicts with the community's interest, we say no, politely, and explain why. In my experience, most reasonable companies accept that, because they also benefit from vLLM being neutral ground where everyone, including their competitors, is willing to contribute.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that when a commercial need genuinely conflicts with the community’s interest, they politely say no.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions limited maintainer bandwidth, but does not explain that demand exceeding their capacity to serve customers enables them to turn down unwanted work.

astra-6.text:
I try to understand whether the conflict is about priorities or about the direction of the project. A commercial customer might need something urgently, while the community has other priorities. In that case, we can discuss who will contribute the engineering work and how to make the solution useful beyond that one customer.

But paying for a feature shouldn’t automatically mean deciding the public roadmap. If a request adds complexity for everyone and only benefits one deployment, I’d look for a way to support it through an extension or a separate integration. The core project needs to remain useful and maintainable for the whole community.

The important thing is to explain those decisions openly. Commercial customers need clear expectations, and community contributors need to know their work and feedback still matter.

r001.rationale: The response discusses managing conflicting requests through prioritization, extensions, and open communication, but does not say it declines commercial customers.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention customer demand exceeding capacity or turning down unwanted work.

sol-6.1.text:
I try to understand the underlying need first. A commercial customer might ask for something very specific to their deployment, while the community needs a solution that is useful across many environments. The question is whether we can find a general design that serves both.

If we can, that’s a good contribution to the open-source project. If the requirement is highly customized, I’d keep that customization separate rather than make everyone carry the complexity. Commercial support matters, but it shouldn’t automatically determine the project’s direction. You need to explain those decisions openly and give community contributors a chance to weigh in.

r001.rationale: The response says commercial needs should not automatically set project direction and that highly customized work should stay separate, but it does not state that customers are declined.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention limited capacity to serve customers as a reason for turning down work.
